title: Rams Cut Kicker Mevis After Missed Calls, Sign Jets’ Grupe to Bolster Special Teams
body:
Los Angeles — The Rams announced a decisive shift on the kicking unit on Tuesday, cutting former fifth‑round pick Harrison Mevis and bringing in Blake Grupe, a former New York Jets practice‑squad specialist. The move, confirmed by NFL insiders, underscores a growing impatience in the organization after a series of costly miscues in recent games and signals a fresh attempt to stabilize a position that has become a liability on the field.

Mevis, who entered the league in 2022 and spent the past two seasons largely on the Rams’ roster, struggled to find consistency during a rough stretch that saw the team miss several field goals and extra points in crucial moments. In the most recent loss, his missed 48‑yard attempt and a botched snap on a 38‑yard try contributed directly to a three‑point deficit that proved decisive. While Mevis has shown flashes of a strong leg in practice, the Rams’ coaching staff concluded that the margin for error in a competitive NFC West is too thin to allow further experimentation.

Enter Blake Grupe, a 25‑year‑old kicker who spent the 2023 season on the Jets’ practice squad after a brief stint on their active roster. Grupe’s résumé includes a solid college career at the University of Texas at El Paso, where he posted a 84.5 percent field‑goal conversion rate and demonstrated reliability inside 40 yards. Though he has yet to log regular‑season snaps in the NFL, his performance in preseason games and intra‑team workouts earned him a reputation as a disciplined, technically sound kicker with a calm demeanor under pressure—traits the Rams hope will translate to immediate on‑field results.

The decision arrives amid a broader evaluation of special teams under new head coach Sean McVay, who is known for demanding precision across all phases of the game. McVay’s staff has been scrutinizing every facet of the Rams’ roster, and the kicker position has risen to the top of that list after a series of close defeats where special‑teams errors proved costly. By swapping Mevis for Grupe, the Rams aim to inject fresh competition into the role, potentially prompting both players to elevate their performance in training camp and preseason matchups.

Analysts note that the Rams’ willingness to make a mid‑season roster adjustment at kicker reflects a rare urgency. In recent years, most teams have preferred to ride out a struggling kicker through a slump rather than disrupt the unit’s chemistry. However, the Rams’ recent defensive lapses and offensive inconsistencies have amplified the impact of every missed point, prompting a more aggressive approach. Moreover, the move could have salary‑cap implications; releasing Mevis frees up a modest amount of cap space that can be redirected toward depth at other positions, while Grupe’s practice‑squad contract is financially minimal.

Looking ahead, Grupe will have limited time to assimilate the Rams’ special‑teams schemes before the regular season resumes. He will need to quickly develop rapport with the long snapper and holder, adapt to the unique wind patterns at SoFi Stadium, and prove his mettle in high‑pressure situations. If he can deliver reliable kicks and avoid the missteps that plagued Mevis, the Rams could solidify a critical component of their game plan and give McVay another tool to manage close contests. Conversely, if Grupe struggles, the Rams may be forced to revisit the market again, potentially targeting veteran free agents or exploring further practice‑squad options.

The Rams’ gamble on Blake Grupe illustrates a broader trend in the NFL: teams are increasingly willing to make swift personnel changes when special‑teams performance directly influences win‑loss outcomes. As the season unfolds, all eyes will be on Los Angeles to see whether this calculated risk pays off and helps the franchise reclaim its status as a perennial contender in a fiercely competitive division.
